title: Reduction of Order
short: Use one known solution to find another.

blocks.html: For a repeated root the second solution $te^{rt}$ seemed to come from nowhere. Reduction of order is the systematic version: if you know one solution $y_1$ of a second-order linear homogeneous equation, it produces a second one, even when the coefficients are not constant.
Put $y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = 0$ in standard form and set $y = v(t)\,y_1(t)$. Then $w = v'$ satisfies a first-order equation, and $$y_2 = y_1\int \frac{e^{-\int p\,dt}}{y_1^{2}}\,dt.$$

With $y = vy_1$: $y' = v'y_1 + vy_1'$ and $y''$ $= v''y_1 + 2v'y_1' + vy_1''$. Substituting, $$v\underbrace{(y_1'' + py_1' + qy_1)}_{=\,0} + v''y_1 + v'(2y_1' + py_1) = 0.$$ The terms with $v$ itself cancel because $y_1$ is a solution. With $w = v'$: $y_1w' + (2y_1' + py_1)w = 0$, which separates: $\frac{w'}{w} = -\frac{2y_1'}{y_1} - p$, so $w = \frac{e^{-\int p\,dt}}{y_1^{2}}$. Integrate once more for $v$.

blocks.title: Where $te^{rt}$ comes from
blocks.q: $y_1 = e^{3t}$ solves $y'' - 6y' + 9y = 0$. Find a second solution.

blocks.title: An exponential appears
blocks.q: $y_1 = t$ solves $(1 - t)y'' + ty' - y = 0$ for $t < 1$. Find $y_2$.
steps: Standard form: $p = \frac{t}{1 - t} = -1 + \frac{1}{1 - t}$, so $\int p\,dt = -t - \ln(1 - t)$ and $e^{-\int p\,dt} = (1 - t)e^{t}$.

blocks.html: Reading $p$ before dividing by the coefficient of $y''$ (using $-3$ instead of $-\frac{3}{t}$ in the second example) gives a wrong $w$. Also remember $y_2 = v\,y_1$, not $v$ alone. Any constant multiple of $y_2$, or $y_2$ plus a multiple of $y_1$, is just as good, so constants of integration can be dropped. Finish by substituting $y_2$ into the equation.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $y_1 = t^{2}$ and $y_2 = t^{2}\ln t$ from the second example. The factor $v = \ln t$ bends $y_2$ away from $y_1$, so neither is a multiple of the other.

blocks.html: This connects with the Wronskian. The function $w = v'$ found here is $\left(\frac{y_2}{y_1}\right)' = \frac{W}{y_1^{2}}$, and $e^{-\int p\,dt}$ is exactly Abel's formula for $W$. So reduction of order says: choose the Wronskian you want, then integrate $\frac{W}{y_1^{2}}$ and multiply by $y_1$. The same substitution $y = vy_1$ also works for the nonhomogeneous equation; then the first-order equation for $w$ gains a right side.
